slides.title: Propositional logic
slides.sub: Chapter 5 · Taking conditions apart like a construction kit, not like a spell
slides.main: Formal logic makes a condition understandable before it runs, not after the bug.

captions: Propositional logic: opens the logic part of the course
Every time you write a condition in an if statement, you are doing propositional logic
A tangled inversion, an argument about the precedence of "and" and "or", a suddenly green test — the territory of the chapter
We take Boolean expressions apart like a construction kit, not like a spell

frames.text: this is already a formula of propositional logic

body.text: Every condition in an if statement is propositional logic: arguments about the precedence of "and" and "or" and suddenly green tests are the territory of the chapter.

slides.title: What a proposition is
slides.sub: The atom of the whole chapter
slides.main: The closest relative of a proposition in code is an expression of Boolean type in a condition.

captions: Let's start with the proposition — the atom of the whole chapter
A statement that is objectively either true or false: there is no third option
Not propositions: a question, a command, and "this sentence is false" — a paradox, it cannot be assigned a value
In code the closest relative is an expression of Boolean type: anything you can put in a condition

frames.text: can be put in an if

body.text: A paradox is a phrase that cannot be assigned either of the two values. An ordinary proposition has no third option.

slides.title: Three basic operations
slides.sub: Compound propositions are built from them
slides.main: The mathematical "or" is inclusive: the case "both are true" suits it too.

captions: Compound propositions are built from simple ones with three basic operations
"Not" flips the truth
"And" is true only when both parts are true
"Or" is true when at least one part is true — including the case of both
Precedence: "not" binds tighter than "and", "and" tighter than "or" — parentheses are for unambiguity

body.text: Precedence: "not" binds tighter than "and", "and" tighter than "or". Parentheses in complex conditions are written not for beauty but for unambiguity.

slides.title: How to read a truth table
slides.sub: The behavior of a formula in all possible cases
slides.short: How to read a truth table
slides.main: For n variables there are 2ⁿ rows: a full enumeration of inputs gives a guaranteed answer.

captions: A truth table writes out the behavior of a formula in all possible cases
For two variables there are four rows: 11, 10, 01, 00
For three — eight; for n variables — 2ⁿ: the power set is back
A full enumeration of inputs gives a guarantee: a formula of five variables is checked with 32 rows

body.text: Two variables — four rows, three — eight, five — thirty-two: the same count as for the power set in the chapter on sets. A formula of five variables is checked with thirty-two rows, not by intuition.

slides.title: Implication: if, then
slides.sub: The fifth operation, the most counterintuitive
slides.main: In code implication hides in every early return: if the argument is empty — return an error.

captions: The fifth operation is the most counterintuitive — implication "if, then"
The first part is the premise, the second the consequence
"If it rains, then the pavement is wet"
The pavement is wet from a sprinkler too — the promise is not violated: it says only "rain ⇒ wet"
In code implication hides in an early return: if the argument is empty — return an error

body.text: The promise is one-sided: the pavement may be wet from a sprinkler, and the implication is not violated — it promises only that rain makes the pavement wet.

slides.title: The catch of a false premise
slides.sub: When the premise is false, the implication is true automatically
slides.short: The catch of a false premise
slides.main: "All elements satisfy the condition" on an empty array honestly returns true.

captions: And now the catch that everyone trips over
When the premise is false, the implication is true — automatically, for any consequence
"If two is greater than three, then I am a ballerina": two is not greater than three — formally true
The contract "if the input is invalid, abort" is not violated when the input is valid — the check quietly passed
all() on an empty array honestly returns true: no elements — no violators

frames.text: "invalid input ⇒ abort" — a false premise, the contract is intact

slides.title: Equivalence in tests
slides.sub: "If and only if" — the sixth operation
slides.main: Equivalence is a two-way implication: the second follows from the first and back.

captions: The sixth operation is equivalence: "if and only if"
True when both parts coincide: both true or both false
It is a two-way implication: the second follows from the first and back
In tests: the expected result equals the actual one — otherwise the test is red
In refactoring: "the new condition is equivalent to the old one" — the tables matched in every row

body.text: And in refactoring too: "the new condition is equivalent to the old one" means that their truth tables matched in every row.

slides.title: Tautology and contradiction
slides.sub: Classes of formulas by the whole truth table
slides.main: A tautological condition is a dead check, a contradictory condition is an unreachable branch.

captions: Formulas fall into classes according to the whole truth table
A tautology is true in all rows: "it is raining or it is not raining"
A contradiction is false in all rows: "rain and no rain at the same time"
In code: a tautology is a dead check, a contradiction is an unreachable branch
Linters clean this up on their own, but in reasoning contradictions hide more often than it seems

body.text: Linters and compilers clean such places up automatically, but in architectural reasoning — in "always", "never" and "either this or that" — contradictions hide more often than it seems.

slides.title: Laws of the algebra of logic
slides.short: Laws of the algebra of logic
slides.main: These laws are the algebra of conditions: expressions are simplified as mechanically as numbers.

captions: As with sets, logical operations have laws, and most of them look natural
The order of "and" does not matter, nor does the order of "or"; with the same operation, parentheses as convenient
A double negation cancels: "it is not true that it is not true" is the original statement
Distributivity: a common factor is taken out of parentheses and put back — for "and" and for "or"
The algebra of conditions: expressions are simplified as mechanically as numbers in a school exercise

frames.text: parentheses with the same operation — as convenient
"it is not true that it is not true" — the same statement

body.text: The order with the same operation does not matter, a double negation cancels, distributivity works for both "and" and "or" — a common factor is taken out of parentheses, as in school algebra.

slides.title: De Morgan's laws
slides.sub: The instruction for inverting conditions in code
slides.main: Everyone who has turned a condition inside out for an early return has applied De Morgan.

captions: The most useful laws are again De Morgan's, now for logic
"It is not true that a and b" = "not a or not b"; "it is not true that a or b" = "not a and not b"
An everyday check: did not take the umbrella and the keys at the same time — so did not take the umbrella or did not take the keys
The instruction for inverting conditions: "not" of an "and" gives an "or" of negations, of an "or" — an "and" of negations
Everyone who turned a condition inside out for an early return applied De Morgan

frames.text: "and" ↔ "or" swap places, the negation goes inside
did not take both at once
↔ if not a or not b:
↔ if not a and not b:
if not a or not b:
an early return — De Morgan in action

body.text: An everyday check: "did not take the umbrella and the keys at the same time" is the same as "did not take the umbrella or did not take the keys". The negation of an "and" gives an "or" of negations, of an "or" — an "and".

slides.title: Short-circuiting in code
slides.sub: A practical bridge into programming languages
slides.main: Here logic is not a metaphor but a working contract: protection from null references and lazy evaluation.

captions: A practical bridge into programming languages is short-circuiting
"And" and "or" are evaluated lazily: if the left part decides the outcome, the right part is not evaluated at all
The check "the user exists and the name is longer than five": on a null reference the second part will not run
It is a direct consequence of the tables: for "and" the result is known when the left part is false
Here logic is a working contract: protection from null references and lazy evaluation rest on it

frames.text: logic is not a metaphor but a contract

body.text: It is not a compiler trick but a direct consequence of the truth tables: the result of "and" is already known when the left part is false.

slides.title: Three daily habits
slides.sub: How to apply this every day
slides.main: Formal logic is a way to make a condition understandable before it runs, not after the bug.

captions: How do you apply all this daily?
First: simplify conditions with the laws before writing — fewer negations and less nesting
Second: test by the truth table — each row of a condition is a separate test case
Third: read other people's conditions aloud — "at least one is not satisfied" is clearer than a wall of exclamation marks
Formal logic is a way to make a condition understandable before it runs, not after the bug

frames.text: branch coverage = coverage of table rows
"at least one of the two is not satisfied"

body.text: Branch coverage is in essence the coverage of the rows of the table.

slides.title: Summary: the vocabulary of logic
slides.main: Propositional logic is the vocabulary on which predicates and quantifiers will be built next.

captions: Summing up the chapter
The vocabulary: proposition, "not", "and", "or", implication, equivalence, tables, tautologies, De Morgan, short-circuiting
These are rules for handling individual statements — at this level half of the tangled conditions get cleaned up
Next — predicates and quantifiers: speaking about all elements at once or at least about one
This is how program properties are formulated: no negatives, an index exists, any request on time

frames.text: no negatives · an index exists · any request on time

body.text: Next — predicates and quantifiers: statements about all numbers at once or at least about one.
